deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. It is a fair-copy of lecture notes on ancient history, continuing the scheme from the previous folio: Section 1, 'Geschichte der ältesten asiatischen und afrikanischen Reiche vor Cyrus'. The page names the Assyrians, Medes and Babylonians as the peoples of Asia and then opens 'I. Assyrische Geschichte'. Its content, in order:
(1) The legendary founder Assur, son of Sem, is dated c. 2100 BC.
(2) His son Ninus builds Nineveh and subjugates Babylonia, Media and Armenia; Persia and Phoenicia are added above the line.
(3) Ninus's wife Semiramis beautifies Babylon and makes it her residence.
(4) The real Assyrian imperial period is dated later, around 800 BC, with expansion westward.
(5) A list of kings follows:
  a. Phul (c. 773) campaigns against Menahem of Samaria, who buys him off with 1000 talents of silver (2 Kings 15:19).
  b. Tiglatpileser (740) is called in by Ahaz of Judah against Damascus and Samaria (2 Kings 16).
  c. Salmanasser (c. 720) campaigns against Hoshea of Samaria, who tried to free himself by seeking help in Egypt; Salmanasser besieges the king of Samaria.
The sentence is continued on the next page (fall of Samaria and deportation, then Sanherib and Assarhaddon).
No derivations, formulas or computations occur. The bundle label 'HB.Lagrange1816' notwithstanding, this is history-lecture material in the style of Göttingen courses of c. 1800, for example Heeren's universal history or Gatterer/Spittler-type schemata. The handwriting and content suggest a student's notebook, possibly copied by or for Gauss or bound with his papers. Attribution to Gauss as author of the content is doubtful.
errors: Historical, not mathematical: the page lists Phul (Pul) and Tiglatpileser as distinct kings, with Phul c. 773. Modern Assyriology identifies Pul with Tiglath-Pileser III (r. 745–727 BC). This was a standard error of early-19th-century textbooks.
Assur 'son of Sem' at 2100 BC, and Ninus/Semiramis as founders, are biblical-legendary chronology (Genesis, Ctesias/Diodorus), not historical. This was standard for the period.

Shalmaneser V reigned 727–722 BC; 'c. 720' is approximately right. The capture of Samaria (722/721) was completed under Sargon II, who is omitted from the list. This was again typical of the era's sources.

results.what: Outline chronology of the Assyrian kings (Phul, Tiglatpileser, Salmanasser) and their relations with Israel/Samaria and Judah, based on 2 Kings 15–17
results.usually_credited_to: Standard textbook material of the late 18th/early 19th c. (e.g., A. H. L. Heeren, J. C. Gatterer)

deep.surprise_reason: The page contains only routine historical lecture notes (ancient Near Eastern history) with no mathematical content. Most likely it is a student notebook rather than original Gauss work.
transcription_corrections: The insertions above the line are correctly placed: 'Medien' after 'Babylonien', 'Persien, Phönicien' above 'Armenien', 'war Semiramis und' after 'Seine Gemahlin'. The reading is: 'unterwarf sich Babylonien, Medien und Armenien [Persien, Phönicien]. Seine Gemahlin war Semiramis und die verschönerte Babylon'.
'die fällt zwischen[?] um 800 a. C.' probably reads 'Sie fällt zwischen[?]/ungefähr um 800 a. C.'; the start of the line is capitalised 'Sie'.
'Er unternahm einen Zug gegen den König von Samaria, Menahem' is confirmed by context (2 Kings 15:19: 1000 talents of silver).
'Dieser wollte sich frei machen, schickte aber Gesandte nach Aegypten' is uncertain; it could read 'suchte aber Hülfe in Aegypten', with 'Gesandte' as the interlinear insertion.
'Salmanasser belagerte [Samarien;] den König von Samarien' is continued on the next page ('nahm er weg').
